TAXI STRIKE: COUNTING COSTS

By: Marion Edmunds | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Cape Town counts the cost of the taxi strike which cost the Western Cape billions of rands and reset the power balance on the roads

Unique Selling Point:
The precarious truce between Cape Town City and Provincial authorities on the one hand, and the taxi industry on the other masks the deep scars left on the psyche of the Mother City. We will zoom in on themes of despair and hope as we look at the impact of the strike on Philippi East, a crime-ridden suburb caught in the middle of the strike, where community assets were targeted by looters, but were held back by civic activists, connecting together around Phillippi Village. At the same time we will check in on the state of power play over who controls the Cape's roads, and whether the compromises over law-enforcement hammered out at the negotiating table will be enough to sustain a peaceful future for those who live and work on the contested southern most tip of Africa.

Summary:
INSERT:
We will explore this story of trauma and hope through the lens of the people of Philippi East, one of the worst affected areas during the strike.

We will interview the CEO of the Philippi Village, Bushra Razak, who runs this foreign-funded business incubator which operates as an NGO in one of Cape Town’s most crime-wracked townships. During the strike, Razak monitored the violence, mapping hot spots and doing her utmost to protect the village of containers, each of which houses a small business. On the fifth and sixth day of the strike, Bushra and her team were sorely tested as the violence increase. She summoned a tactical unit to protect the premises, but they were attacked and could not get there. Things got worse when a mob fronted by a bulldozer started to wreak havoc and destruction as it moved towards the village. Razack then worked her phones to contact all community members she knew including Amaphela (Avanza taxi) drivers to calm the situation which they did with some success, although five containers were burnt.

Under 40 years, Durban-born Bushra Razack, is an award-winning community development specialist, with experience of working in communities across Africa. But her leadership skills were sorely tested by the strike; she had to dig deep to handle the violence threatening the assets of the NGO, and take her leadership theory and implement it intuitively and in real-time to protect the business campus, which as a foreign funded entrepreneurial hub was a target for the looters, along with the local library and community hall.

We will also interview the Village’s security head Vuyokazi Tinise who was on the coalface of negotiations with the looters at the gate, so to speak. We will also interview seamstress Nomafu Mdlambuzi whose sewing business in one of the containers in Philippi Village which was raided during the strike. Criminals stole her sewing machines, finished orders ready for collection, fridge and microwave. They only thing they left was the embroidery machine which was heavy, so they smashed it instead. Her business supports 18 family members. She is now picking up the pieces of the incident.

We will interview Mandla Hermanus, the chairperson of SANTACO, about the experience of the strike and press him to answer particular questions, which include why they eventually settled for an agreement which mirrored the one on the table a week earlier, and how they account for the violence. But we will also explore with him the cost to the taxi industry which was estimated as over a R100 million, and will now be potentially increased by a damages claim the city expects to put in against SANTACO. We will check with him how far the negotiations have gone in securing a lasting peace and what SANTACO has learnt from the strike.

We have secured an interview with Cape Town’s Mayor, Geordin-Hill Lewis, to ask him for his personal experience of the strike, and what his guiding principles were to lead through it to an outcome on the other side. We will ask him to be precise about the damages claim, and to explain how it will be calculated, given that complainants have been told there is a single case number for all the incidents logged under the taxi strike, and some of those complainants are bemused as to how to track this case, and what is happening with the investigation. We will check with him how far the negotiations have got in securing a lasting peace and what the city and the province will do differently as a result.

These two characters knelt together at the St George’s Cathedral prayer for peace, but came from different social and political spaces and were on the opposite sides of the strike.

Other interviewees:
Cognisant of the need to keep a muscular silhouette of a story, I have not committed yet to more interviews. However, these are options, some of whom have already agreed to do an interview.

1) Penelope Mthiyane, baker at Chalry’s Bakery who we interviewed for the last story and whose grandson, who went missing and has now returned, is suffering trauma. We could interview her to get more details of what actually happened to her grandson, now that she knows, and how she and her grandson are dealing with the PTSD. He was very frightened to go back to school for fear of the men who pushed him around when he tried and failed to catch the school bus on that day.

2) A family member of the slain doctor on zoom from the UK. I have put in a request with the UK embassy and they are going to talk to the family on Carte Blanche’s behalf on Monday the 11th. They say for the sake of sensitivity they will not do it earlier. I have also contacted a family member by email.

3) The mediator Adrian Vlok. I listened to his interview with Lezanne and found it very useful and interesting but at the same time he is an expert and is somewhat detached from the nitty gritty of the action. One way of managing his input, is to reflect it in the questions and the script rather than interviewing him directly.

4) A small time taxi operator who is willing to share his side of the story. Mandla Hermanus has promised to look for such a person but he has not provided details yet.

5) An outlier – maybe Marius Fransman, the disgraced ANC politician who has been using the strike to boost his profile, was one of the voices encouraging the strikers on the day it started and who has been releasing statements on the SANTACO media whatsapp group. He may be able to provide the dynamic tension of the opposing view as I understand he owns taxis as well. But this may not fit in.

6) Riccardo Mackenzie, the lead negotiator with the taxi industry, and provincial MEC for mobility but we did interview him last time, and interviewing one city/province voice, in this case the mayor, should be sufficient.

BACKGROUND/HISTORY
From Thursday afternoon the 2nd of August to the following Friday, Cape Town was in turmoil as violence gripped the poorest part of the city, and encroached on the freedom of the road, paralysing the city’s economy, terrifying its citizens, keeping half a million learners out of school, closing hospitals and clinics, damaging almost 500 vehicles and leaving six innocent people dead, including a visiting British doctor. It was earlier estimated that the strike cost the Western Cape Economy R5 billion and the City of Cape Town R18 million.

After on and off negotiations and a series of court cases forced all parties into an agreement the major players have been trying to iron out their disagreements over the law to prevent this sort of upheaval from happening again. And those affected by the violence have been trying to rebuild their lives. In both of these acts of recovery, there are seeds of hope of a new relationship and better working relationships on the road.


Further information:
When we go to Philippi East we will need security.

I also have the number of the Community Police Forum liaison, but I have been advised to start at Nyanga Police station and ask for a police escort because the criminality is so brazen there. Philippi Villlage is in the centre of Philippi. It is a colourful business incubator in containers, funded for use of the community and provides a centre for entrepreneurs, with wifi and facilities.
https://www.facebook.com/thephilippivillage/posts/for-rentour-beautiful-and-colorful-container-walk-is-suitable-for-both-retail-an/2897281020500850/

I have secured the main interviews for the 11th and 12th of September. I believe that I will get more information/leads to follow up on the shoot which might lead to other interviews or angles which I can do without a presenter. The talks to finalise the working arrangement between the taxi industry and the authorities are set to conclude on the week of the 18th of September but no commitments have been made. It depends if they are running it as fourteen working days or two weeks. This may influence broadcast time.

Referring to the storytelling workshop:
Story A – the story of Philippi Village in the strike, representing in broad terms the community of Cape Town
Story B – the story of the power play between the authorities represented by the Mayor and the taxi industry represented by Mandla Hermanus of SANTACO
Story C – the story of one of the other smaller characters (lighter, more personal and intimate as a relief)

Dynamic Tension: A dreadful thing happened but in that crisis, hope is born of maybe crafting new relationship between the state and the taxi industry

Press Release:


Taxi Strike: The Aftermath
In August this year, a week-long taxi strike in Cape Town left a trail of destruction. Six people were killed and millions of rands of damage was done to public and private property. At the centre of the stand-off was a demand that taxi impoundments should be limited and thousands of confiscated vehicles released. Chaos and violence spilled onto the streets and, for eight days, commuters were stranded and local businesses put at risk. But despite taxi bosses pushing hard to force the city to loosen its iron grip on the industry, officials held firm. Now, the precarious truce between the City of Cape Town on one hand and the taxi industry on the other masks the deep suspicion with which they view each other.



Producer: Marion Edmunds | Presenter: Erin Bates

Script:


FINAL SCRIPT – TAXI STRIKE: Counting the Cost #6439
Producer: Marion Edmunds
Presenter: Erin Bates
TX: 24 September 2023

(VO) THERE IS LONG-RUNNING TENSION BETWEEN THOSE WHO PROVIDE MOST OF THE TRANSPORT TO THE PEOPLE OF THE WESTERN CAPE, REPRESENTED BY THE TAXI ASSOCIATION SANTACO….

AND THOSE WHO ENFORCE THE LAWS OF THE ROAD…

LAST MONTH, STRIFE BETWEEN TAXI BOSSES AND THE AUTHORITIES EXPLODED INTO A VIOLENT STRIKE.

ERIN BATES: This is what rush hour traffic looks like in Cape Town on any given weekday afternoon but transport networks ground to a halt, paralysed during a deadly and devastating taxi strike last month. It left commuters not only terrified but stranded.

(VO) IN THE TOWNSHIP OF PHILIPPI, AN NGO OPERATING FROM A RENOVATED CONCRETE FACTORY WENT ON HIGH ALERT.

SECURITY MANAGER, VUYOKAZI TINISE, DID NOT SLEEP THAT WEEK.

Vuyokazi Tinise
Security Manager: Philippi Village
My worry was about the premises because I know what it holds inside, and I know the assets that are inside.

(VO) PHILIPPI VILLAGE PROVIDES A SANCTUARY FOR THE COMMUNITY – FOR WORK AND PLAY.

BUT LIKE OTHER PUBLIC SPACES ACROSS THE CAPE, IT WAS SUDDENLY VULNERABLE – A TARGET FOR CRIMINALS EMBOLDENED BY THE TAXI STAYAWAY.

Vuyokazi Tinise
Security Manager: Philippi Village
Those eight days were like a year. It was so hectic, it was too much stressful. You feel sick, although you are not sick, but because of the shock of the things that are happening.

(VO) JUST GETTING HOME ON THAT FIRST DAY WAS AN ORDEAL FOR VUYOKAZI’S COLLEAGUES.

UPSOUND: This is the hub where the community starts connecting.

(VO) FOUR STAFF MEMBERS ATTEMPTED TO LEAVE THE PREMISES WITH A BABY IN THE CAR, WHILE ON THE PHONE TO PHILIPPI VILLAGE CEO, BUSHRA RAZACK.

Bushra Razack
CEO: Philippi Village
They said that they drove down the road with the most horrific experiences, they saw a bus on fire, a taxi on fire, people throwing rocks and throwing stones. One of our colleagues spoke about a massive piece of granite that went into the car in front of them which they saw make contact with the driver’s head, blood, the car veering off the road, the situation escalated very quickly.

(VO) BUSHRA USED HER COMMUNITY NETWORKS, BUILT UP OVER YEARS, TO SECURE HER STRANDED STAFF AND HELP THEM TO SAFETY.

Bushra Razack
CEO: Philippi Village
Our team were able to reach out to associations, to community groups, who were able to make contact with these drivers and say, please leave this group of people alone.

(VO) ACROSS THE CAPE, OTHER PEOPLE WERE NOT SO LUCKY.
SIX MEN WERE MURDERED.
COUNTLESS VEHICLES TORCHED AND DAMAGED.
THE LOCAL BUS SERVICE, GOLDEN ARROW, LOST NINE VEHICLES.
THE MAYOR GEORDIN HILL-LEWIS SAYS THE CITY IS STILL ASSESSING THE DAMAGE.

Geordin Hill-Lewis
Executive Mayor: City of Cape Town
We've calculated that and we're still adding up at 30 million Rand already. And that is why we are taking civil action against SANTACO to recover those. I know that Golden Arrow’s losses will be in similar amounts …

So the damages will will be many, many 10s of millions. The damage to the to the economy more broadly is much greater than that even because of the huge inconvenience to 10s of 1000s of commuters

(VO) THE MAYOR CAN SEE CAPE TOWN’S LARGEST TAXI RANK FROM HIS OFFICE WINDOW.
IT’S HERE THAT TRAFFIC OFFICERS AND TAXI DRIVERS CLASHED EARLY IN AUGUST.
THE VIRAL IMAGES FED A PENT-UP RAGE AMONGST TAXI OPERATORS.

(VO) BUT THE BAD FEELING RUNS DEEPER THAN A SINGLE INCIDENT – TAXI BOSSES AND THE AUTHORITIES HAD BEEN IN DIFFICULT TALKS FOR MONTHS.

ERIN BATES: There are many sticking points operating licences, routes, subsidies, but the issue that generates the most anxiety is the impoundment of taxis breaking the law.

(VO) CONFISCATION OF TAXIS OR IMPOUNDMENT IS A LEGAL SANCTION - BUT BITTERLY CONTESTED.

Geordin Hill-Lewis
Executive Cape Town Mayor
There are certain fundamental principles at stake here. ……And they can't be subject to, you know, wink and a handshake. And one of them is that, you know, you can't negotiate away which parts of the law you don't like.

(VO) YET BY THE END OF JULY, CAPE TOWN’s TAXI BOSSES HAD HAD ENOUGH, SAYS SANTACO WESTERN CAPE CHAIRPERSON, MANDLA HERMANUS.


Mandla Hermanus,
Chairperson of SA National Taxi Council, (SANTACO) Western Cape
The impoundments were continuing at an increasing rate, because by that time, we had had over 6000 of our vehicles, having been impounded. And as a direct result of that we had 488 vehicles where it was being repossessed by the banks, because the operators were no longer able to meet their financial obligations.

(VO) OUT OF POCKET, OUT OF PATIENCE, TAXI DRIVERS BLOCKADED ROUTES AND INTIMIDATED ROAD-USERS…

(VO) AND ALMOST IMMEDIATELY VANDALS SEIZED THE OPPORTUNITY TO TRASH AND LOOT.

Geordin Hill-Lewis
Executive Cape Town Mayor
We have more than 300 separate case numbers for cases already open either by us or by SAPS themselves.. … more than 100 where people have already appeared in court. Most unfortunately, have been let go.

(VO) WHILE THE POLICE ARE INVESTIGATING HUNDREDS OF INDIVIDUAL INCIDENTS, THE CITY IS BUILDING A BIGGER CASE AGAINST SANTACO.

ERIN BATES: Where's the chain of evidence, Where's the proof that SANTACO is in your view liable?

Geordin Hill-Lewis
Executive Cape Town Mayor
We've gone back and looked at I think 11 previous taxi strikes in in Cape Town over the years, and every single one of them include exactly the same pattern of violence ….perhaps what we didn't have, in all those other cases was a much wider expanse of of cameras available to the city, many 1000s of cameras that the city now has on our all of our freeways. So we are busy stitching together as much evidence as we can possibly gather to try and make exactly that case.

(VO) SANTACO REJECTS RESPONSIBILITY FOR THE VIOLENCE.
THEY HAVE ALREADY RECEIVED SOME WRITTEN CLAIMS, INCLUDING ONE FOR R25 MILLION.

Mandla Hermanus,
Chairperson of SA National Taxi Council, (SANTACO) Western Cape
Just after the stayaway ended , we had already received like emails – it was as if people were being mobilised to say here’s an email address. You had your car window broken, please email here….… we know that rock throwing happens every dayWe do not believe if there is a stay away then all the criminality that normally happens is then put on hold.

(VO) BUT IT WAS ALL THE MORE DANGEROUS IN CRIME-RIDDEN HOTSPOTS LIKE PHILIPPI.

(VO) LATE ONE NIGHT A MOB OPERATING A BULLDOZER TARGETED SIXTY SMALL BUSINESSES SITUATED IN STREET-FACING SHIPPING CONTAINERS IN PHILIPPI VILLAGE.

Vuyokazi Tinise
Security Chief: Philippi Village
So everything happened so fast, it was like a movie, because it was just a boom, boom, boom. And then after that the crowd go inside, Take things so quick,

(VO) BUSHRA AND THE SECURITY TEAM CALLED ON A NEARBY BUSINESS FOR BACK UP – AND WHILE FIVE CONTAINERS WERE VANDALISED, THE REST WERE SAVED. BUT EVEN THAT WAS A HEAVY PRICE TO PAY.

ERIN BATES: Rebuilding and repairing damage is one thing, but recovering from the violence, the trauma and loss is not easy for the people and communities most affected.

(VO) ONE OF THOSE WAS NOMAFU MDLAMBUZI, A PHILIPPI VILLAGE FASHION DESIGNER WHO SUPPORTS HER EXTENDED FAMILY MAKING GARMENTS AND DOING EMBROIDERY. HER CONTAINER WAS LOOTED BY THE MOB ON THE BULLDOZER.

Nomafu Mdlambuzi
Fashion Designer: Philippi Village
We came running and when I got here, I nearly died. It was like a dead person to me. I didn't believe it. And I still don't believe it even now, if it happens, I will be really hurt….. Actually the taxi strike just killed my plans. And I was so so sad. Especially when we are home, seeing my mother crying. That is a part of the thing that I never wanted in life.

THE LOOTERS TOOK HER FINISHED ORDERS, HER MATERIAL AND SOME OF HER MACHINES.
THEY DROPPED HER HEAVY EMBROIDERY MACHINE ON THEIR WAY OUT, DAMAGING IT.

Nomafu Mdlambuzi
Fashion Designer: Philippi Village
It took me two weeks to come back. Two weeks to come back. Even my mom would push me and say, " No, I'm not going there because every time I entered it, I just got a picture of people taking what's not belonging on them. And it really kills me.

(VO) DURING THE EIGHT DAYS OF THE STRIKE, SANTACO TRIED TO DISTANCE ITSELF FROM THE VIOLENCE TO APPEASE AN ENRAGED PUBLIC.

Mandla Hermanus,
Chairperson of SA National Taxi Council, (SANTACO) Western Cape
We always say the law enforcement is intelligence driven. …they should have been able to do anticipate some of those things

(VO) THE STRIKE HAS RAISED SANTACO’S PROFILE IN THE PROVINCE. POLITICAL PARTIES AND INDUSTRY BODIES ARE QUEUING UP TO MEET THE EXECUTIVE.
BUT TRUST WITH LOCAL GOVERNMENT IS TAKING TIME TO BUILD, DESPITE ONGOING NEGOTIATIONS.

Mandla Hermanus,
Chairperson of SA National Taxi Council, (SANTACO) Western Cape
The government was at the forefront of saying these are thugs, these are criminals, these are mafias, these are extortionists, these are less than decent human beings, simply because we're saying you cannot impound my vehicle because it's got two people more than it should have.

(VO) THE MAYOR SAYS HE WILL HOLD SANTACO TO ACCOUNT THROUGH THE CRIMINAL JUSTICE SYSTEM, THROUGH COURT ORDERS AND THE BALLOONING DAMAGES CLAIM.

Geordin Hill-Lewis
Executive Cape Town Mayor
I mean, many 1000s of South Africans, not just Capetonians have been in touch with with us to say how much the taxi strike has given them hope. And that's a very strange thing to say… if we want to be successful as a country in the future, we have to stand by the rule of law.

(VO) THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ALL PARTIES REMAINS FRAGILE
BUT THEY DID REACH AN AGREEMENT TO PREVENT SUCH CHAOS FROM HAPPENING AGAIN - A MANDATORY 36 HOUR NOTICE PERIOD BEFORE A STRIKE.

Geordin Hill-Lewis
Executive Cape Town Mayor
Day One Cam B
The safety and escalation mechanisms I think are a real step forward in a way that will will, I hope, show its worth in years to come. And I think will will come to be copied across the industry as we go further.

(VO) IN THE LAST WEEKS, THE PEOPLE AT PHILIPPI VILLAGE HAVE BEEN SHARING THEIR TAXI STRIKE STORIES.
REVIEWING THE CRISIS, FINDING THEIR CALM.
AND WORKING ON WAYS TO BUILD EVEN STRONGER COMMUNITY BONDS AS THE BEST PROTECTION FOR WHEN THIS HAPPENS AGAIN.

PROMO ONE:

You can't negotiate away which parts of the law you don't like.
(VO) A FRAGILE TRUCE AFTER A DEVASTATING STRIKE
The government was at the forefront of saying these are thugs, these are criminals, … these are less than decent human beings.

Everything happened so fast, it was like a movie, because it was just a boom, boom, boom.
(VO) ORDINARY PEOPLE CAUGHT UP IN AN EXTRAORDINARY TAXI STRIKE.
I just got a picture of people taking what's not belonging on them. And it really killed me.


PROMO THREE:

(VO) WHERE THERE IS SMOKE, THERE MAY BE FIRE

We are busy stitching together as much evidence as we can possibly gather.

(VO) THE CITY OF CAPE TOWN BUILDS A MULTI-MILLION RAND DAMAGES CASE AGAINST ITS TRANSPORT PARTNER, THE TAXI INDUSTRY.

We will zoom in on themes of despair and hope as we look at the impact of the strike on Philippi East, a crime-ridden suburb caught in the middle of the strike, where community assets were targeted by looters, but were held back by civic activists, connecting together around Phillippi Village. At the same time we will check in on the state of power play over who controls the Cape's roads, and whether the compromises over law-enforcement hammered out at the negotiating table will be enough to sustain a peaceful future for those who live and work on the contested southern most tip of Africa. Summary: INSERT: We will explore this story of trauma and hope through the lens of the people of Philippi East, one of the worst affected areas during the strike. We will interview the CEO of the Philippi Village, Bushra Razak, who runs this foreign-funded business incubator which operates as an NGO in one of Cape Town’s most crime-wracked townships. During the strike, Razak monitored the violence, mapping hot spots and doing her utmost to protect the village of containers, each of which houses a small business. On the fifth and sixth day of the strike, Bushra and her team were sorely tested as the violence increase. She summoned a tactical unit to protect the premises, but they were attacked and could not get there. Things got worse when a mob fronted by a bulldozer started to wreak havoc and destruction as it moved towards the village. Razack then worked her phones to contact all community members she knew including Amaphela (Avanza taxi) drivers to calm the situation which they did with some success, although five containers were burnt. Under 40 years, Durban-born Bushra Razack, is an award-winning community development specialist, with experience of working in communities across Africa. But her leadership skills were sorely tested by the strike; she had to dig deep to handle the violence threatening the assets of the NGO, and take her leadership theory and implement it intuitively and in real-time to protect the business campus, which as a foreign funded entrepreneurial hub was a target for the looters, along with the local library and community hall. We will also interview the Village’s security head Vuyokazi Tinise who was on the coalface of negotiations with the looters at the gate, so to speak. We will also interview seamstress Nomafu Mdlambuzi whose sewing business in one of the containers in Philippi Village which was raided during the strike. Criminals stole her sewing machines, finished orders ready for collection, fridge and microwave. They only thing they left was the embroidery machine which was heavy, so they smashed it instead. Her business supports 18 family members. She is now picking up the pieces of the incident. We will interview Mandla Hermanus, the chairperson of SANTACO, about the experience of the strike and press him to answer particular questions, which include why they eventually settled for an agreement which mirrored the one on the table a week earlier, and how they account for the violence. But we will also explore with him the cost to the taxi industry which was estimated as over a R100 million, and will now be potentially increased by a damages claim the city expects to put in against SANTACO. We will check with him how far the negotiations have gone in securing a lasting peace and what SANTACO has learnt from the strike. We have secured an interview with Cape Town’s Mayor, Geordin-Hill Lewis, to ask him for his personal experience of the strike, and what his guiding principles were to lead through it to an outcome on the other side. We will ask him to be precise about the damages claim, and to explain how it will be calculated, given that complainants have been told there is a single case number for all the incidents logged under the taxi strike, and some of those complainants are bemused as to how to track this case, and what is happening with the investigation. We will check with him how far the negotiations have got in securing a lasting peace and what the city and the province will do differently as a result. These two characters knelt together at the St George’s Cathedral prayer for peace, but came from different social and political spaces and were on the opposite sides of the strike. Other interviewees: Cognisant of the need to keep a muscular silhouette of a story, I have not committed yet to more interviews. However, these are options, some of whom have already agreed to do an interview. 1) Penelope Mthiyane, baker at Chalry’s Bakery who we interviewed for the last story and whose grandson, who went missing and has now returned, is suffering trauma. We could interview her to get more details of what actually happened to her grandson, now that she knows, and how she and her grandson are dealing with the PTSD. He was very frightened to go back to school for fear of the men who pushed him around when he tried and failed to catch the school bus on that day. 2) A family member of the slain doctor on zoom from the UK. I have put in a request with the UK embassy and they are going to talk to the family on Carte Blanche’s behalf on Monday the 11th. They say for the sake of sensitivity they will not do it earlier. I have also contacted a family member by email. 3) The mediator Adrian Vlok. I listened to his interview with Lezanne and found it very useful and interesting but at the same time he is an expert and is somewhat detached from the nitty gritty of the action. One way of managing his input, is to reflect it in the questions and the script rather than interviewing him directly. 4) A small time taxi operator who is willing to share his side of the story. Mandla Hermanus has promised to look for such a person but he has not provided details yet. 5) An outlier – maybe Marius Fransman, the disgraced ANC politician who has been using the strike to boost his profile, was one of the voices encouraging the strikers on the day it started and who has been releasing statements on the SANTACO media whatsapp group. He may be able to provide the dynamic tension of the opposing view as I understand he owns taxis as well. But this may not fit in. 6) Riccardo Mackenzie, the lead negotiator with the taxi industry, and provincial MEC for mobility but we did interview him last time, and interviewing one city/province voice, in this case the mayor, should be sufficient. BACKGROUND/HISTORY From Thursday afternoon the 2nd of August to the following Friday, Cape Town was in turmoil as violence gripped the poorest part of the city, and encroached on the freedom of the road, paralysing the city’s economy, terrifying its citizens, keeping half a million learners out of school, closing hospitals and clinics, damaging almost 500 vehicles and leaving six innocent people dead, including a visiting British doctor. It was earlier estimated that the strike cost the Western Cape Economy R5 billion and the City of Cape Town R18 million. After on and off negotiations and a series of court cases forced all parties into an agreement the major players have been trying to iron out their disagreements over the law to prevent this sort of upheaval from happening again. And those affected by the violence have been trying to rebuild their lives. In both of these acts of recovery, there are seeds of hope of a new relationship and better working relationships on the road. Further information: When we go to Philippi East we will need security. I also have the number of the Community Police Forum liaison, but I have been advised to start at Nyanga Police station and ask for a police escort because the criminality is so brazen there. Philippi Villlage is in the centre of Philippi. It is a colourful business incubator in containers, funded for use of the community and provides a centre for entrepreneurs, with wifi and facilities. https://www.facebook.com/thephilippivillage/posts/for-rentour-beautiful-and-colorful-container-walk-is-suitable-for-both-retail-an/2897281020500850/ I have secured the main interviews for the 11th and 12th of September. I believe that I will get more information/leads to follow up on the shoot which might lead to other interviews or angles which I can do without a presenter. The talks to finalise the working arrangement between the taxi industry and the authorities are set to conclude on the week of the 18th of September but no commitments have been made. It depends if they are running it as fourteen working days or two weeks. This may influence broadcast time. Referring to the storytelling workshop: Story A – the story of Philippi Village in the strike, representing in broad terms the community of Cape Town Story B – the story of the power play between the authorities represented by the Mayor and the taxi industry represented by Mandla Hermanus of SANTACO Story C – the story of one of the other smaller characters (lighter, more personal and intimate as a relief) Dynamic Tension: A dreadful thing happened but in that crisis, hope is born of maybe crafting new relationship between the state and the taxi industry Extra Budget Items: Security - was not TX Date: 0000-00-00 Press Release: Taxi Strike: The Aftermath In August this year, a week-long taxi strike in Cape Town left a trail of destruction. Six people were killed and millions of rands of damage was done to public and private property. At the centre of the stand-off was a demand that taxi impoundments should be limited and thousands of confiscated vehicles released. Chaos and violence spilled onto the streets and, for eight days, commuters were stranded and local businesses put at risk. But despite taxi bosses pushing hard to force the city to loosen its iron grip on the industry, officials held firm. Now, the precarious truce between the City of Cape Town on one hand and the taxi industry on the other masks the deep suspicion with which they view each other. Producer: Marion Edmunds | Presenter: Erin Bates Script: FINAL SCRIPT – TAXI STRIKE: Counting the Cost #6439 Producer: Marion Edmunds Presenter: Erin Bates TX: 24 September 2023 (VO) THERE IS LONG-RUNNING TENSION BETWEEN THOSE WHO PROVIDE MOST OF THE TRANSPORT TO THE PEOPLE OF THE WESTERN CAPE, REPRESENTED BY THE TAXI ASSOCIATION SANTACO…. AND THOSE WHO ENFORCE THE LAWS OF THE ROAD… LAST MONTH, STRIFE BETWEEN TAXI BOSSES AND THE AUTHORITIES EXPLODED INTO A VIOLENT STRIKE. ERIN BATES: This is what rush hour traffic looks like in Cape Town on any given weekday afternoon but transport networks ground to a halt, paralysed during a deadly and devastating taxi strike last month. It left commuters not only terrified but stranded. (VO) IN THE TOWNSHIP OF PHILIPPI, AN NGO OPERATING FROM A RENOVATED CONCRETE FACTORY WENT ON HIGH ALERT. SECURITY MANAGER, VUYOKAZI TINISE, DID NOT SLEEP THAT WEEK. Vuyokazi Tinise Security Manager: Philippi Village My worry was about the premises because I know what it holds inside, and I know the assets that are inside. (VO) PHILIPPI VILLAGE PROVIDES A SANCTUARY FOR THE COMMUNITY – FOR WORK AND PLAY. BUT LIKE OTHER PUBLIC SPACES ACROSS THE CAPE, IT WAS SUDDENLY VULNERABLE – A TARGET FOR CRIMINALS EMBOLDENED BY THE TAXI STAYAWAY. Vuyokazi Tinise Security Manager: Philippi Village Those eight days were like a year. It was so hectic, it was too much stressful. You feel sick, although you are not sick, but because of the shock of the things that are happening. (VO) JUST GETTING HOME ON THAT FIRST DAY WAS AN ORDEAL FOR VUYOKAZI’S COLLEAGUES. UPSOUND: This is the hub where the community starts connecting. (VO) FOUR STAFF MEMBERS ATTEMPTED TO LEAVE THE PREMISES WITH A BABY IN THE CAR, WHILE ON THE PHONE TO PHILIPPI VILLAGE CEO, BUSHRA RAZACK. Bushra Razack CEO: Philippi Village They said that they drove down the road with the most horrific experiences, they saw a bus on fire, a taxi on fire, people throwing rocks and throwing stones. One of our colleagues spoke about a massive piece of granite that went into the car in front of them which they saw make contact with the driver’s head, blood, the car veering off the road, the situation escalated very quickly. (VO) BUSHRA USED HER COMMUNITY NETWORKS, BUILT UP OVER YEARS, TO SECURE HER STRANDED STAFF AND HELP THEM TO SAFETY. Bushra Razack CEO: Philippi Village Our team were able to reach out to associations, to community groups, who were able to make contact with these drivers and say, please leave this group of people alone. (VO) ACROSS THE CAPE, OTHER PEOPLE WERE NOT SO LUCKY. SIX MEN WERE MURDERED. COUNTLESS VEHICLES TORCHED AND DAMAGED. THE LOCAL BUS SERVICE, GOLDEN ARROW, LOST NINE VEHICLES. THE MAYOR GEORDIN HILL-LEWIS SAYS THE CITY IS STILL ASSESSING THE DAMAGE. Geordin Hill-Lewis Executive Mayor: City of Cape Town We've calculated that and we're still adding up at 30 million Rand already. And that is why we are taking civil action against SANTACO to recover those. I know that Golden Arrow’s losses will be in similar amounts … So the damages will will be many, many 10s of millions. The damage to the to the economy more broadly is much greater than that even because of the huge inconvenience to 10s of 1000s of commuters (VO) THE MAYOR CAN SEE CAPE TOWN’S LARGEST TAXI RANK FROM HIS OFFICE WINDOW. IT’S HERE THAT TRAFFIC OFFICERS AND TAXI DRIVERS CLASHED EARLY IN AUGUST. THE VIRAL IMAGES FED A PENT-UP RAGE AMONGST TAXI OPERATORS. (VO) BUT THE BAD FEELING RUNS DEEPER THAN A SINGLE INCIDENT – TAXI BOSSES AND THE AUTHORITIES HAD BEEN IN DIFFICULT TALKS FOR MONTHS. ERIN BATES: There are many sticking points operating licences, routes, subsidies, but the issue that generates the most anxiety is the impoundment of taxis breaking the law. (VO) CONFISCATION OF TAXIS OR IMPOUNDMENT IS A LEGAL SANCTION - BUT BITTERLY CONTESTED. Geordin Hill-Lewis Executive Cape Town Mayor There are certain fundamental principles at stake here. ……And they can't be subject to, you know, wink and a handshake. And one of them is that, you know, you can't negotiate away which parts of the law you don't like. (VO) YET BY THE END OF JULY, CAPE TOWN’s TAXI BOSSES HAD HAD ENOUGH, SAYS SANTACO WESTERN CAPE CHAIRPERSON, MANDLA HERMANUS. Mandla Hermanus, Chairperson of SA National Taxi Council, (SANTACO) Western Cape The impoundments were continuing at an increasing rate, because by that time, we had had over 6000 of our vehicles, having been impounded. And as a direct result of that we had 488 vehicles where it was being repossessed by the banks, because the operators were no longer able to meet their financial obligations. (VO) OUT OF POCKET, OUT OF PATIENCE, TAXI DRIVERS BLOCKADED ROUTES AND INTIMIDATED ROAD-USERS… (VO) AND ALMOST IMMEDIATELY VANDALS SEIZED THE OPPORTUNITY TO TRASH AND LOOT. Geordin Hill-Lewis Executive Cape Town Mayor We have more than 300 separate case numbers for cases already open either by us or by SAPS themselves.. … more than 100 where people have already appeared in court. Most unfortunately, have been let go. (VO) WHILE THE POLICE ARE INVESTIGATING HUNDREDS OF INDIVIDUAL INCIDENTS, THE CITY IS BUILDING A BIGGER CASE AGAINST SANTACO. ERIN BATES: Where's the chain of evidence, Where's the proof that SANTACO is in your view liable? Geordin Hill-Lewis Executive Cape Town Mayor We've gone back and looked at I think 11 previous taxi strikes in in Cape Town over the years, and every single one of them include exactly the same pattern of violence ….perhaps what we didn't have, in all those other cases was a much wider expanse of of cameras available to the city, many 1000s of cameras that the city now has on our all of our freeways. So we are busy stitching together as much evidence as we can possibly gather to try and make exactly that case. (VO) SANTACO REJECTS RESPONSIBILITY FOR THE VIOLENCE. THEY HAVE ALREADY RECEIVED SOME WRITTEN CLAIMS, INCLUDING ONE FOR R25 MILLION. Mandla Hermanus, Chairperson of SA National Taxi Council, (SANTACO) Western Cape Just after the stayaway ended , we had already received like emails – it was as if people were being mobilised to say here’s an email address. You had your car window broken, please email here….… we know that rock throwing happens every dayWe do not believe if there is a stay away then all the criminality that normally happens is then put on hold. (VO) BUT IT WAS ALL THE MORE DANGEROUS IN CRIME-RIDDEN HOTSPOTS LIKE PHILIPPI. (VO) LATE ONE NIGHT A MOB OPERATING A BULLDOZER TARGETED SIXTY SMALL BUSINESSES SITUATED IN STREET-FACING SHIPPING CONTAINERS IN PHILIPPI VILLAGE. Vuyokazi Tinise Security Chief: Philippi Village So everything happened so fast, it was like a movie, because it was just a boom, boom, boom. And then after that the crowd go inside, Take things so quick, (VO) BUSHRA AND THE SECURITY TEAM CALLED ON A NEARBY BUSINESS FOR BACK UP – AND WHILE FIVE CONTAINERS WERE VANDALISED, THE REST WERE SAVED. BUT EVEN THAT WAS A HEAVY PRICE TO PAY. ERIN BATES: Rebuilding and repairing damage is one thing, but recovering from the violence, the trauma and loss is not easy for the people and communities most affected. (VO) ONE OF THOSE WAS NOMAFU MDLAMBUZI, A PHILIPPI VILLAGE FASHION DESIGNER WHO SUPPORTS HER EXTENDED FAMILY MAKING GARMENTS AND DOING EMBROIDERY. HER CONTAINER WAS LOOTED BY THE MOB ON THE BULLDOZER. Nomafu Mdlambuzi Fashion Designer: Philippi Village We came running and when I got here, I nearly died. It was like a dead person to me. I didn't believe it. And I still don't believe it even now, if it happens, I will be really hurt….. Actually the taxi strike just killed my plans. And I was so so sad. Especially when we are home, seeing my mother crying. That is a part of the thing that I never wanted in life. THE LOOTERS TOOK HER FINISHED ORDERS, HER MATERIAL AND SOME OF HER MACHINES. THEY DROPPED HER HEAVY EMBROIDERY MACHINE ON THEIR WAY OUT, DAMAGING IT. Nomafu Mdlambuzi Fashion Designer: Philippi Village It took me two weeks to come back. Two weeks to come back. Even my mom would push me and say, " No, I'm not going there because every time I entered it, I just got a picture of people taking what's not belonging on them. And it really kills me. (VO) DURING THE EIGHT DAYS OF THE STRIKE, SANTACO TRIED TO DISTANCE ITSELF FROM THE VIOLENCE TO APPEASE AN ENRAGED PUBLIC. Mandla Hermanus, Chairperson of SA National Taxi Council, (SANTACO) Western Cape We always say the law enforcement is intelligence driven. …they should have been able to do anticipate some of those things (VO) THE STRIKE HAS RAISED SANTACO’S PROFILE IN THE PROVINCE. POLITICAL PARTIES AND INDUSTRY BODIES ARE QUEUING UP TO MEET THE EXECUTIVE. BUT TRUST WITH LOCAL GOVERNMENT IS TAKING TIME TO BUILD, DESPITE ONGOING NEGOTIATIONS. Mandla Hermanus, Chairperson of SA National Taxi Council, (SANTACO) Western Cape The government was at the forefront of saying these are thugs, these are criminals, these are mafias, these are extortionists, these are less than decent human beings, simply because we're saying you cannot impound my vehicle because it's got two people more than it should have. (VO) THE MAYOR SAYS HE WILL HOLD SANTACO TO ACCOUNT THROUGH THE CRIMINAL JUSTICE SYSTEM, THROUGH COURT ORDERS AND THE BALLOONING DAMAGES CLAIM. Geordin Hill-Lewis Executive Cape Town Mayor I mean, many 1000s of South Africans, not just Capetonians have been in touch with with us to say how much the taxi strike has given them hope. And that's a very strange thing to say… if we want to be successful as a country in the future, we have to stand by the rule of law. (VO) THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ALL PARTIES REMAINS FRAGILE BUT THEY DID REACH AN AGREEMENT TO PREVENT SUCH CHAOS FROM HAPPENING AGAIN - A MANDATORY 36 HOUR NOTICE PERIOD BEFORE A STRIKE. Geordin Hill-Lewis Executive Cape Town Mayor Day One Cam B The safety and escalation mechanisms I think are a real step forward in a way that will will, I hope, show its worth in years to come. And I think will will come to be copied across the industry as we go further. (VO) IN THE LAST WEEKS, THE PEOPLE AT PHILIPPI VILLAGE HAVE BEEN SHARING THEIR TAXI STRIKE STORIES. REVIEWING THE CRISIS, FINDING THEIR CALM. AND WORKING ON WAYS TO BUILD EVEN STRONGER COMMUNITY BONDS AS THE BEST PROTECTION FOR WHEN THIS HAPPENS AGAIN. PROMOS: PROMO ONE: You can't negotiate away which parts of the law you don't like. (VO) A FRAGILE TRUCE AFTER A DEVASTATING STRIKE The government was at the forefront of saying these are thugs, these are criminals, … these are less than decent human beings. PROMO TWO: Everything happened so fast, it was like a movie, because it was just a boom, boom, boom. (VO) ORDINARY PEOPLE CAUGHT UP IN AN EXTRAORDINARY TAXI STRIKE. I just got a picture of people taking what's not belonging on them. And it really killed me. PROMO THREE: (VO) WHERE THERE IS SMOKE, THERE MAY BE FIRE We are busy stitching together as much evidence as we can possibly gather. (VO) THE CITY OF CAPE TOWN BUILDS A MULTI-MILLION RAND DAMAGES CASE AGAINST ITS TRANSPORT PARTNER, THE TAXI INDUSTRY.

Razack then worked her phones to contact all community members she knew including Amaphela (Avanza taxi) drivers to calm the situation which they did with some success, although five containers were burnt. Under 40 years, Durban-born Bushra Razack, is an award-winning community development specialist, with experience of working in communities across Africa. But her leadership skills were sorely tested by the strike; she had to dig deep to handle the violence threatening the assets of the NGO, and take her leadership theory and implement it intuitively and in real-time to protect the business campus, which as a foreign funded entrepreneurial hub was a target for the looters, along with the local library and community hall. We will also interview the Village’s security head Vuyokazi Tinise who was on the coalface of negotiations with the looters at the gate, so to speak. We will also interview seamstress Nomafu Mdlambuzi whose sewing business in one of the containers in Philippi Village which was raided during the strike. Criminals stole her sewing machines, finished orders ready for collection, fridge and microwave. They only thing they left was the embroidery machine which was heavy, so they smashed it instead. Her business supports 18 family members. She is now picking up the pieces of the incident. We will interview Mandla Hermanus, the chairperson of SANTACO, about the experience of the strike and press him to answer particular questions, which include why they eventually settled for an agreement which mirrored the one on the table a week earlier, and how they account for the violence. But we will also explore with him the cost to the taxi industry which was estimated as over a R100 million, and will now be potentially increased by a damages claim the city expects to put in against SANTACO. We will check with him how far the negotiations have gone in securing a lasting peace and what SANTACO has learnt from the strike. We have secured an interview with Cape Town’s Mayor, Geordin-Hill Lewis, to ask him for his personal experience of the strike, and what his guiding principles were to lead through it to an outcome on the other side. We will ask him to be precise about the damages claim, and to explain how it will be calculated, given that complainants have been told there is a single case number for all the incidents logged under the taxi strike, and some of those complainants are bemused as to how to track this case, and what is happening with the investigation. We will check with him how far the negotiations have got in securing a lasting peace and what the city and the province will do differently as a result. These two characters knelt together at the St George’s Cathedral prayer for peace, but came from different social and political spaces and were on the opposite sides of the strike. Other interviewees: Cognisant of the need to keep a muscular silhouette of a story, I have not committed yet to more interviews. However, these are options, some of whom have already agreed to do an interview. 1) Penelope Mthiyane, baker at Chalry’s Bakery who we interviewed for the last story and whose grandson, who went missing and has now returned, is suffering trauma. We could interview her to get more details of what actually happened to her grandson, now that she knows, and how she and her grandson are dealing with the PTSD. He was very frightened to go back to school for fear of the men who pushed him around when he tried and failed to catch the school bus on that day. 2) A family member of the slain doctor on zoom from the UK. I have put in a request with the UK embassy and they are going to talk to the family on Carte Blanche’s behalf on Monday the 11th. They say for the sake of sensitivity they will not do it earlier. I have also contacted a family member by email. 3) The mediator Adrian Vlok. I listened to his interview with Lezanne and found it very useful and interesting but at the same time he is an expert and is somewhat detached from the nitty gritty of the action. One way of managing his input, is to reflect it in the questions and the script rather than interviewing him directly. 4) A small time taxi operator who is willing to share his side of the story. Mandla Hermanus has promised to look for such a person but he has not provided details yet. 5) An outlier – maybe Marius Fransman, the disgraced ANC politician who has been using the strike to boost his profile, was one of the voices encouraging the strikers on the day it started and who has been releasing statements on the SANTACO media whatsapp group. He may be able to provide the dynamic tension of the opposing view as I understand he owns taxis as well. But this may not fit in. 6) Riccardo Mackenzie, the lead negotiator with the taxi industry, and provincial MEC for mobility but we did interview him last time, and interviewing one city/province voice, in this case the mayor, should be sufficient. BACKGROUND/HISTORY From Thursday afternoon the 2nd of August to the following Friday, Cape Town was in turmoil as violence gripped the poorest part of the city, and encroached on the freedom of the road, paralysing the city’s economy, terrifying its citizens, keeping half a million learners out of school, closing hospitals and clinics, damaging almost 500 vehicles and leaving six innocent people dead, including a visiting British doctor. It was earlier estimated that the strike cost the Western Cape Economy R5 billion and the City of Cape Town R18 million. After on and off negotiations and a series of court cases forced all parties into an agreement the major players have been trying to iron out their disagreements over the law to prevent this sort of upheaval from happening again. And those affected by the violence have been trying to rebuild their lives. In both of these acts of recovery, there are seeds of hope of a new relationship and better working relationships on the road.
